messages.subject: point transects
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I have data collected from fixed observations points, and was wondering if=20
the data could be suitable to estimate density considernig the observation=20
points as point transects.=20

I have 8 different observation points randomly distributed in the survey=20
area. Observations were done simountaneously from all observation points.=20
>From each point a regular scan of the observed area was done every three=20
minutes. During each of these events the radial distance to each animal=20
seen was taken. Observation sessions lasted 1hour and a half for a total of =

30 scans for each point.=20

Of course there is a high possibility that many animals were counted=20
repeatedly, from the same observation point or animals seen repeatedly in=20
different points. There are also many scans with no observation at all. Do=20
you think this kind of data is suitable for a robust point transect=20
analysis or not? Should I consider the 30 scans as =93survey effort=94 for e=
ach=20
point transect or how?

I would be glad of any idea and imput you can give me!

Achaz von Hardenberg
Alpine Wildlife Research Centre
Gran Paradiso National Park, Italy

--

messages.subject: Re: Covariates and sample size
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 23 Aug 2005 15:57:03 +0100, Manuel Spinola wrote:

> >Hi all,

> >I am using observers as a covariate but one of the observers only have 3
> >detections.  Should I eliminate this observer from my data set? or should
> >I pool this observer with another observer?
> >Thank you in adavance.

> >Manuel Spinola

Hi Manuel, list,

I think there's no perfect answer, although I'd be interested to hear if
anyone else feels differently.

If you assigned observers to transects at random then there should be no
bias associated with dropping their effort.  Presumably if they saw few
objects then this is only a small part of the total effort, so variance
should not be increased greatly.

Alternatively, you could leave the observer in - you'll probably find that
the covariate value associated with this observer has a large variance,
which is what one would expect.  So long as the estimated scale parameter is
not really silly you could be content with this.

Another alternative would be to group your observers into categories
(experienced/inexperienced or some such) and try those.

Lastly, ask yourself why you are using covariates in the first place.  If
you are simply interested in an overall estimate of abundance then you may
be better not using observer as a covariate at all, and relying on pooling
robustness to give you an unbiased estimate of abundance.  The only reason
to use covariates in this case is to increase precision, and the component
of the variance coming from the detection function is typically small, so
you won't get much gain.  If you do want to try covariates then dividing
observers into categories might be as far as you want to go (and then using
AIC to tell you whether this is "better" than no covariates).

If, on the other hand, you are interested in density by region or by year
then a global detection function with no covariates will potentially produce
biased estimates of detection probability by region or year.  If you have
different observers in different regions or years, this may have motivated
you to try observer as a covariate.  However, an alternative is to try
region or year as the covariate, effectively pooling the observers within
the region or year.  Again pooling robustness says you should get an
estimate for each region or year that has little bias (although using region
or year as a covariate is less flexible than full stratification so there
may be some bias).   So, if you don't have enough observations from all
observers, you could in this situation try year or region as a covariate
instead and let AIC tell you whether this is "better" than the global CDS
detection function.

As an aside, in this situation (when you want to fit a global detection
function using a covariate but estimate density by stratum) you need to tick
on both the global and stratum boxes in Detection function line of the
Estimate tab in the Model Definition.  Look in the online help index under
"Estimating the detection function at multiple levels in MCDS" for more on
this.  You probably knew this already, but many people do not!

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Request for help
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

We are preparing for a Rapid Assessment Survey of two important marine=20
turtle foraging habitats in Albania=94 to be held in Albania, from October=20
15th, 2005. The project aims to survey and clarify the sea turtle status=20
at sea (feeding grounds) in two Albanian lagoons. The fieldwork will focus=20
on Rapid Underwater Site Assessments (RUSA) at various locations in those=20
areas based on the information gathered from fishermen surveys=20
(Questionnaires and interviews with local fishermen) and previous=20
scientific data. A series of random dives will be conducted at different=20
locations in selected areas. We plan to use the Line Transect method and=20
Distance V.5 software. Does anyone have relative experience or recommend=20
reference/bibliography for such surveys or has experience for such=20
modelling with Distance V.5.?
=20
Thanks for your help.
=20

Vassilis Kouroutos
Marine Biologist

MEDASSET-Mediterranean Association to Save the Sea Turtles

messages.subject: Line Transect analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello List.

I am relatively new to the joys of distance, and any comments would be much
appreciated.  In 2000 and 2005, around 140 1km squares were surveyed on
Salisbury Plain to look at bird populations in the area. The methods
followed the UK National Breeding Bird Survey, which consists of walking
two one-kilometre lines through each square and recording birds in distance
categories. Each square was visited twice in each year (i.e. 4km walked).
During 2000 the standard categories were used (0-25m 25-100m and 100m+),
however this was increased to 5 in 2005 so that better models could be
fitted to the data (0-10m; 10-25m; 25-100m; 100-250m; 250m+). Each survey
line was split up into five different 200-metre sections and habitats were
recorded on this basis.

The first part of the analysis is to look at density changes between the
two surveys. It is key to investigate changes within the five different
regions of the Plain, as they have received different management.  For
this, I only used squares surveyed in both years and confined it to the 0-
25m and 25-100m distance categories. The analysis was undertaken with a
Half Normal model and a Global detection function as this was thought not
to vary across area.  For a number of species there was an increase in raw
count data, but a significant decline in density estimate due to large
difference in the models fitted between years. The question is whether
recorder effects should be investigated, or whether it is good enough to
look at an average surveyor in both years. Is there a way of both looking
at Stratum densities (using a Global detection function) while also
investigating recorder effects?  Each recorder had the same overall survey
effort, however the same recorder was not always used over both visits to a
square.

Secondly, identifying habitat associations. The survey sample is the
kilometre square, however habitats were recorded on a 200m-section basis
(10 per square). Obviously, these are not independent. Any ideas on how
this should be treated in the analysis.

Regards Andrew Stanbury

--

messages.subject: Re: Line Transect analysis
messages.body_plain:
Andrew, in principle, you're getting absolute estimates of abundance, and
observer differences won't affect this.  You have adjusted for
detectability, which includes any differences in observers.  However, the
number of intervals in 2000 was very small (3, effectively 2 for smaller
species), so some bias can be anticipated.  Hence you may want to play
around with observer effects.  If you use the multiple covariate distance
sampling engine of Distance, you can include observer as a factor type
covariate.

You can classify 200m sections by habitat type, and then estimate density
for each habitat type, by stratifying by habitat type.  You'll need to
enter data separately by 200m section and include a field for habitat type
to do this.

Steve Buckland
